It looks like every project by default has a standing token with read privileges. It never expires and its not opt-in. Unless I'm missing something, that seems ridiculous.
Rollbar and similar (Logz.io, Datadog, New Relic, etc) are such honeypots - JACKPOTS - for anyone capable of harpooning their way in that I'm surprised they aren't targeted more frequently.

Rollbar breach notice wording is concerning; commenter wanted explicit confirmation that GitHub credentials for source code integration were not compromised, since 'including' suggests the breach could be wider.

Rollbar staff (Brian) responded: customer credentials for third-party integrations (GitHub, Slack, JIRA) are stored encrypted with a key not stored in the database, so those were not exposed in the breach.

Why aren't they taking action to not copy access tokens to their data warehouse? Best practice would be to store such keys encrypted to prevent breaches from non-production datasource access or direct production database access.

Entire Rollbar customer base received test emails from internal testing, apparently caused by an email aliasing issue where sending to team@ automatically blasted a newsletter with the email's content.

The idea of sending an email to team@ which then automatically, without any further input, blasts a newsletter with the email's content seems badly designed... ripe for accidental or deliberate misuse.
